notes.meaning: This happened after Saul's son Ishbosheth died. By then David had ruled only the tribe of Judah from Hebron for about seven and a half years. Now all the tribes came to him. "Your own flesh and blood" was a way of saying they belonged together as one people. David was no stranger to them, and they wanted him.

The leaders gave two more reasons to make David king. First, he had already led Israel's army well, even while Saul was king. Second, God had chosen him. God called David a shepherd of His people. That is a title God also uses for Himself, the Chief Shepherd.

David and the leaders made a covenant, a solemn agreement before God. David promised to protect the people, and they promised to stay loyal to him. Matthew Henry notes that David agreed to rule by law, though he could have demanded total power. The public anointing, a ceremony of pouring oil on the new king, showed the whole nation accepting him. It also fulfilled what God had said long before through Samuel.

David's first big act as king of all Israel was to march on Jerusalem. Back then it was called Jebus, and the Jebusites still held it. The city sat on neutral ground between Judah and the northern tribes. That made it a wise choice for the capital of a united nation.

The Jebusites mocked David and said he could never get in. Their scorn only made David more determined, and he took the fortress of Zion. Matthew Henry links this hill to Psalm 2:6: "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion." Taking this city laid the groundwork for all that came after.

David promised the top army post to whoever led the attack. Joab went up first and won it. Joab was already one of David's captains, but now he became commander over the whole army. Some think Joab had lost favor after he killed Abner, so this brave act won back his place. Only Chronicles tells us this detail.
David moved into the fortress and made it his home. That is why it was called the City of David. Jerusalem now became the royal city.

David built new parts of the city around the fortress. Joab was given the job of repairing the older part that was damaged in the attack. The word used means to "bring back to life," here meaning to rebuild ruins. Some older writers think Joab also became the governor of that part of the city.

David kept growing stronger. The real reason was that the LORD of Hosts was with him. ("LORD of Hosts" means the Lord who commands heaven's armies.) God had prepared David over many years. David did not give the credit to his armies but to God.

Now the writer lists David's chief warriors. These men helped make David king and then helped keep him on the throne. God worked through these people to keep His promise. Many of them had first joined David as people in trouble, in debt, or unhappy, back at the cave of Adullam. By standing with David, they also strengthened themselves.

Jashobeam headed the list as the most honored of the warriors. He killed three hundred men in one battle. Second Samuel 23:8 says eight hundred. Wesley explains that Jashobeam killed 300 himself and others killed 500 more in the chase. Some think a number was miscopied. Matthew Henry says such feats show God's special help.
Next came Eleazar son of Dodo. He was one of "the Three," the top group of David's heroes. Those three men held first rank among all the warriors.

At Pas-dammim the army ran from the Philistines, but a stand was made in a barley field, and the LORD gave a great victory. Comparing this with 2 Samuel 23:9-12, older writers think a few lines were skipped by a copyist here. If so, the barley-field stand was really made by a third hero, Shammah. Either way, the victory is credited to the Lord.

Three of the thirty chief warriors came to David at the cave of Adullam. The Philistine army was camped in the Valley of Rephaim, west of Jerusalem, and they had soldiers posted in Bethlehem, David's hometown. Older writers differ on which three men these were. Some think they were Eleazar and his companions, while others think they were three different heroes.

David longed for a drink from the well at Bethlehem's gate, the water of his childhood home. He probably was not thinking about the Philistine soldiers there. Matthew Henry sees it as a moment of weakness, an idle wish that David later regretted.

The three men fought through the enemy camp to bring David the water. That shows how devoted they were to him. But David would not drink it. To him it was like drinking their blood, because they had risked their lives for it. He poured it out to God as a drink offering, an offering of liquid poured out in worship. Matthew Henry sees four good things here: David was sorry for his careless words, he said no to his own wants, he gave God the best, and he cared deeply about his men.

Abishai, Joab's brother, belonged to a second group of heroes. He killed three hundred men with his spear and became famous. He was honored as the leader of that group. But he never matched the first Three in bravery. Abishai served David in many wars and stood just below Joab among his captains.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 20-25 come from a separate source. They suggest parts may be quoted from a lost poem praising Abishai and Benaiah.

notes.meaning: Benaiah came from Kabzeel, a town in southern Judah. His name means "the LORD has built." He killed two great champions of Moab. On a snowy day he also killed a lion in a pit, perhaps a cave where he had sheltered from the storm. Matthew Henry says such brave deeds needed God's special presence.

Benaiah also faced a huge Egyptian about eight feet tall, with a spear as thick as a weaver's beam. Benaiah had only a club or walking stick. He grabbed the giant's spear and killed him with it. The fight is a lot like David's battle with Goliath.

Deeds like these made Benaiah famous, even though he did not reach the rank of the first Three. Matthew Henry notes that these men won honor by doing good and risking their lives. He adds that those faithful to Jesus, the Son of David, will find their names kept with far greater honor.
